Dendritic cells are the only cells that can do this. They have a variable expression of their MHC and CCR7 molecules depending on their location in the body. In normal tissue they express high levels of the PRR, but low levels of the CCR7. When a pathogen is detected, the dendritic cells undergo a change in expression, expressing high levels of both the PRR and CCR7. This allows them to bridge the gap between the two types of immunity. They can detect the pathogen and also direct the adaptive immune response. They are also the only cells that can travel from the site of infection to the lymph node. This is because they express CCR7, which binds to the stromal cell CCL19 and CCL21. This allows the dendritic cells to travel to the lymph node, where they can present the pathogen to a naive T cell. The naive T cell will then undergo clonal expansion and differentiate into a different type of T cell, which will then travel back to the site of infection to direct the adaptive immune response.

Amnesia is the loss of the ability to recall past events or retain new information.  Amnesia can be an acquired condition, where there is damage to the brain, or it can be a normal part of ageing.  Amnesia can be classified as anterograde or retrograde. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after the damage, whereas retrograde amnesia is the inability to recall memories formed before the damage.  Amnesia can be caused by a number of factors, including:  Damage to the hippocampus or medial temporal lobes of the brain - this is seen in patients with Alzheimer's disease and herpes simplex encephalitis.  Korsakoff syndrome is caused by a thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency and can also cause amnesia.  Anoxia or hypoxia refers to a lack of oxygen to the brain, which can occur as a result of cardiac arrest or brainstem ischaemia. This can cause amnesia due to damage to the hippocampus.  In addition, amnesia can be caused by a brain injury, a meningitis, a stroke, a brain tumour, a metal or viral substance in the blood, or a lesion on the brain surface.  Amnesia can also be a normal part of ageing.  Amnesia can be classified as declarative or non-declarative. Declarative amnesia is the inability to recall facts and events, whereas non-declarative amnesia is the inability to perform motor skills or habits
